Why not write something for those who scratched out improbable livings here? Someone has managed to sow This broken field with stones, it appears, So someone’s scratching it still, Although that Japanese knotweed has edged The tilth. Two wasps in the child Attempt to catch sun on a rail of the bridge. The old local doctor has passed At almost a full decade past ninety. He never seemed depressed. Seventy now, if barely, I consider the field again: Someone will drag these rocks away But they’ll be back. The air smells like rain, Which is fine, the summer’s been much too dry. Nothing is left of the barn But some rusty steel straps in some nasty red osier. The stone fence still looks sound, But even there the knotweed steps over. Hadn’t I pledged an elegy To the old ones who worked here? You couldn’t claim They thrived, exactly, but maybe They likewise scented good wind full of rain, Lifted eyes above this old orchard To the cloud-darkened hills and found their support Somehow, somewhere. No matter, They kept going until they could go no more. The trees’ puckered apples have gathered A flock of birds, and as they alight, They’re full of unseasonable chatter, As if to say that all will be right. The old ones I promised a poem Must have said it too. It’ll be all right. I never knew them. They’re gone. I say it out loud, It’ll be all right. —Caledonia County, Vermont

Here is a polished version, preserving the poem's structure, imagery, and every element of its original meaning:

**Elegy for the Old Ones**

Why not write something for those who scratched
Improbable livings from this ground?
Someone, it seems, has sown
This broken field with stones,
So someone scratches it still,
Though the Japanese knotweed has crept
Along the tilled earth's edge.
Two wasps upon the bridge's rail
Reach for the sun's warmth in the chill.

The old town doctor has passed away,
Nearly a full decade past ninety.
He never once seemed downcast.
Seventy now, if barely so,
I turn to consider the field once more:
Someone will haul these rocks away,
Yet back they'll come. The air smells of rain—
Which suits me well, for summer's run too dry.

Nothing remains of the barn
But rusted steel straps snarled
In an ugly tangle of red osier.
The stone fence still stands sound,
And yet even there the knotweed climbs across.
Had I not pledged an elegy
To the old ones who labored here?
You could not say they thrived,
But perhaps they too caught the good wind full of rain,

Raised their eyes above this aging orchard
To the cloud-darkened hills, and found their sustenance
Somehow, somewhere. No matter—
They carried on until they could go no further.
The trees' shriveled apples have drawn
A flock of birds, and as they settle,
They brim with unseasonable chatter,
As if to say that all will come right.

The old ones I promised a poem
Must have said it too. It'll be all right.
I never knew them. They are gone.
I say it aloud:
It'll be all right.

*—Caledonia County, Vermont*

---

A few notes on the changes: I refined some phrasings for flow and clarity (for instance, "scratched improbable livings from this ground," "crept along the tilled earth's edge," and "snarled in an ugly tangle"), smoothed a likely typo ("the child" rendered as "the chill" to fit the imagery of wasps seeking sun), and tightened rhythm throughout—while keeping the narrative, imagery, and refrain fully intact. If you'd prefer I preserve the original line breaks and wording even more strictly, or lean further into formal rhyme, I'd be glad to adjust.

Why not compose a verse for those who eked out unlikely lives in this place? It seems someone once planted this ruined field with stones, and someone tends it yet, though the Japanese knotweed has crept up against the cultivated soil. Two wasps in the chill try to gather sunlight on the bridge's railing.

The old country doctor died at nearly a decade beyond ninety. He never appeared downhearted. Now myself just past seventy, if only just, I look upon the field once more: someone will haul these stones off, yet they'll return again. There's rain in the scent of the air, which suits me, since the summer has run far too parched.

The barn has vanished entirely, save for a few rusted metal bands lying among some ugly red osier. The stone wall still seems solid, though even there the knotweed climbs across.

Didn't I promise a mourning song for the old folk who labored in this spot? You couldn't say they truly prospered, but perhaps they, too, breathed a fine wet wind, raised their gaze past this ancient orchard toward the cloud-shadowed hills, and drew their strength from somewhere, somehow. It doesn't matter—they carried on until they could carry on no longer.

The shriveled apples on the trees have drawn a gathering of birds, and as they settle down, they're loud with talk out of season, as though declaring everything will turn out fine. The old ones I owed a poem must have voiced this as well. It'll be all right. I never met them. They've passed away. I speak it aloud, It'll be all right.

—Caledonia County, Vermont
outputs.L3:
# An Elegy for the Land's Forgotten Laborers

I feel compelled to write an elegy for the impoverished people who once labored on this difficult, rocky land. Something in me insists upon it—a debt owed to those whose names I never knew but whose presence still lingers in every furrow and fence.

The field itself refuses to forget them. It remains stubbornly persistent, as though determined to undo all human effort. The stones that were cleared with such backbreaking care keep returning, working their way up through the soil season after season. And the invasive knotweed advances without mercy, steadily encroaching upon the cultivated ground and creeping along the stone fences that once marked the boundaries of hope and ownership.

The old farmers who worked this place never truly thrived. Theirs was not a story of prosperity or triumph. Yet they found some form of support in the natural world that surrounded them—some quiet sustenance, some reason to rise again each morning. They persevered against the odds, continuing their labor until their bodies simply could no longer carry them forward.

Even now, the birds gather in the apple trees, filling the air with an unseasonable, reassuring chatter. There is comfort in that sound, a kind of promise woven through it—the sense that everything will, somehow, turn out all right.

And so I find myself, now seventy years old, echoing the reassurance of those departed strangers. Though I never knew them, though we are separated by generations and by lives utterly unlike my own, I repeat their words aloud into the quiet air: *it'll be all right.* It is my way of joining them across the distance, of adding my voice to theirs, and of believing, if only for a moment, that they were right.
outputs.L4:
# The Old Ones

I had promised them a poem, the old ones,
though they are gone now and would not read it.
This broken field is what remains of them,
this abandoned orchard on the Vermont hill
where they wrestled a living from the ground.

Look how the stones persist. Each spring
they rise again through the thawing soil,
patient as the dead, as if the earth itself
were still giving up its buried labor,
the harvest no one asked for and no one wanted.
The old ones gathered them into walls
that lean now, tumbling back toward chaos,
their careful stacking undone by frost and time.

The knotweed has taken the lower meadow,
that stubborn invader with its bamboo canes
and hollow stalks, choking out
whatever the old ones planted. It spreads
the way forgetting spreads, the way a name
gives way to weather and the passing years.
Still, there is a kind of endurance in it,
a life that will not be told it isn't wanted.

The apple trees are half wild now,
gnarled and unpruned, throwing up suckers,
their fruit gone small and bitter on the branch.
Yet they still blossom. Every May
they put out their white flowers as if hoping,
as if the old ones might return
with their ladders and their baskets,
their rough hands that knew the weight of things.

I stand here in the ruin of their work
and think of what it costs to stay alive,
to break the same ground season after season,
to lift the stones and set them back,
to bury the old ones one by one
in the little plot behind the church.
This is the elegy I promised them,
though it is only stones and trees and weeds,
only the plain facts of what they left.

But listen—the birds are talking in the branches,
the chickadees, the sparrows, going on
about their small important business,
and the sound of them is like a consolation.
They do not mourn. They do not know
the field is broken or the old ones gone.
They chatter in the ruined orchard
as if the world were new and whole,
and something in their careless music says
it will go on, whatever we have lost.

It'll be all right, the old ones used to say,
hands on the plow, backs bent to the work,
the words a kind of prayer against despair.
It'll be all right. I say it now
to the empty field, the leaning wall,
the apple trees still blossoming for no one.
The birds take up the phrase and carry it
into the leaves, into the coming dark.
It'll be all right. And maybe it will.
The stones will rise. The blossoms will return.
And I will keep my promise to the dead,
finding in their vanished lives
this quiet, this acceptance, this going on.
outputs.L5:
# Why Someone Might Choose This

Have you ever stopped to wonder **why** certain people make the decisions they do? Every choice we encounter in life carries a hidden story behind it, and understanding that story often reveals more than we expect.

## The Question of "Why"

The word "why" is one of the most powerful questions we can ask. It pushes us beyond surface-level observations and encourages deeper reflection. When we ask "why" about a situation, we begin to uncover motivations, fears, and hopes that shape human behavior. Children ask "why" constantly because they are naturally curious about the world—perhaps we should never lose that instinct.

## When "Someone" Steps Forward

There is always **someone** willing to take the first step. Someone who dares to try something new, to speak up when others stay silent, or to offer help when it's needed most. That someone could be a stranger, a friend, or even you. The beauty of life lies in these individuals who choose to act, to care, and to make a difference—no matter how small the gesture might seem.

## Why "This" Matters

So **this** brings us to an important point: every decision, every action, and every moment matters. This idea—that our choices carry weight—should inspire us to think carefully about how we live. This is not about perfection, but about intention. When we combine curiosity ("why"), courage (that "someone"), and awareness of the present ("this"), we create a foundation for meaningful lives.

## Conclusion

In the end, asking **why**, recognizing that **someone** must act, and understanding that **this** moment counts, all work together to guide us. These three simple words remind us that life is a continuous journey of questioning, choosing, and growing.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a contemplative poem in the voice of an aging person observing an abandoned Vermont farm field, reflecting on the people who once worked the land. Use rhyme and set it in Caledonia County.
counterfactuals.output:
**The Field at Caledonia**

I lean upon this crooked gate
where iron hinges rust and wait,
and watch the field that once was mowed
run wild beside the county road.

The timothy grows tall and free
where Hansen's plow cut faithfully,
and milkweed claims the tired loam
that fed a barn, that fed a home.

I knew the men who worked this ground—
their boots, their oaths, their morning sound,
the clink of pails, the harness creak,
the frost that bit them cheek to cheek.

Old Amos here, he broke the stone,
each spring a harvest all his own,
and stacked the walls that still remain
to hold back nothing but the rain.

His sons went west, or went to war,
or lie beneath the churchyard door,
and no one came to take the scythe
or pay the land its April tithe.

The maples creep in, row by row,
where corn stood sentinel and low,
and birches, white as Sunday shirts,
inherit all the old man's dirts.

I too am fallow, gray, and slow—
I feel the seasons come and go
the way this pasture feels them pass,
a settling down of bone and grass.

Yet something in the ruin sings:
the way the wild returns and clings,
the way the thrush at evening fills
these emptied, unforgotten hills.

So let me lean here while I may
and give the vanished folk their day,
for I am nearly of their kind—
a field the world has left behind.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a rhyming poem about a rocky, overgrown New England field, mortality, and the passage of generations, ending with a repeated reassurance that "it'll be all right."
counterfactuals.output:
**The Field That Kept the Stones**

The old field leans against the hill,
where stone walls tumble, low and still,
and brambles climb the rusted gate
that no one's opened here of late.

The pasture's gone to birch and pine,
to goldenrod and bittersweet vine;
the plow that broke this stubborn ground
lies orange with rust, without a sound.

My grandfather once cleared these rows,
his father too—the story goes—
each summer stacking granite grey,
each winter watching frost heave clay.

They're gathered now beneath the yews
in earth that keeps the names it choose,
their labor swallowed, blade by blade,
by all the green their hands unmade.

I walk here where the apples fall
untended past the leaning wall,
and count the seasons yet to come
when I'll lie quiet, cold, and dumb.

But look—the field is not bereft:
it holds the shape their hands have left.
The wall still marks where meadows part,
a stubborn ledger of the heart.

My children run the tractor-track
and do not fear the coming black;
they laugh where four whole generations
have wintered into earth's foundations.

So let the milkweed take the plain,
the granite gather moss and rain.
What's given up is not what's lost—
the field remembers every cost.

And when at last I take my rest
where fathers sleep beneath the crest,
the wind will move the birch just so,
the same as it did long ago.

So hush, the evening's turning gold,
the field will keep us as we're old,
and keep the ones we hold so tight—
it'll be all right, it'll be all right.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Write an elegy for anonymous hardscrabble farmers who once scratched out a living on a stony Vermont hillside, incorporating imagery of knotweed, an old orchard, apples, and birds.
counterfactuals.output:
# Elegy for the Hillside Farmers

They left no names, only the stubborn evidence
of walls—each stone lifted by a hand now gone
to loam, set fast against the slumping years.
Here they wrestled bread from reluctant ground,
where thin soil clenched around the roots of stones
like a miser's fist, and every furrow cost.

Now knotweed marches where the barn once stood,
its hollow canes a green forgetting, spreading
its bamboo insurrection through the dooryard,
choking the well-lip, climbing the fallen sill.
What they broke their backs to clear returns,
patient and rank, reclaiming all their labor.

Yet the old orchard holds. See how the trees—
arthritic, black-limbed, split by a hundred winters—
still shoulder up their crooked benediction.
In September the wild apples come:
small, sour, freckled, gnarled as the hands
that pressed the seeds, or grafted, or let them fall.

No one gathers now. The windfalls rot
sweet in the frost-bit grass, and the deer come down,
and wasps drone drunk in the fermenting gold,
and the drops thud soft as footsteps in the dusk—
the sound, perhaps, of someone walking out
at evening to survey a modest kingdom.

The birds are all that keep the harvest here:
cedar waxwings mask-faced in the branches,
a jay's blue insolence, the vireo's
untiring question threaded through the leaves.
They take their tithe and scatter it downhill,
sowing new wildness where the tame once grew.

Sleep, then, you nameless ones who worked and vanished.
Your monument is not the leaning stone
nor letters weathered smooth past reading, but
this: that a thing you planted still bears fruit,
still feeds the wandering wing, the passing tongue—
a bitter sweetness, given to the air.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: I want a formal poem with an ABAB-ish rhyme scheme, in the style of a rural New England pastoral elegy, about a narrator in his seventies looking at a broken field and thinking about death and continuity.
counterfactuals.output:
**The Broken Field**

I lean upon the gatepost, gray with rime,
And count the stones the frost has heaved this year.
The field lies broken now, as I in time
Am broken too, though slower, standing here.

My father cleared these acres, row by row,
And piled the glacier's leavings into wall;
I mended what I could of long ago,
But hands grow stiff, and something has to fall.

The alders creep where once the oxen strained,
And bittersweet has climbed the sagging rails.
No plow will turn this dark, unwilling ground;
The barn leans north against the winter gales.

Yet still the woodchuck keeps his ancient right
To sun himself upon the tumbled stone,
And swallows thread the rafters, morning-bright,
As if the ruin were a thing well-grown.

I do not grieve the way a young man would,
Who thinks the fences ought to hold for good.
I know the field was borrowed, not possessed—
A loan the earth calls back when it thinks best.

Some grandson, or some stranger yet unnamed,
May find these boulders half-sunk in the loam
And wonder at the hands that once had tamed
This crooked pasture, made of it a home.

Let him. The maples I will never see
Will drop their keys into the yielding sod;
The field goes on, indifferent and free,
And I go with it, back into the god

Of seasons, who unmakes to make again.
The frost that breaks the wall will break the man—
And still, come April, in the melting rain,
Green things will rise, as green things always can.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a poem set in a decaying Vermont farm landscape—rusty barn straps, a stone fence, red osier, an old orchard—that meditates on impermanence and quietly consoles itself.
counterfactuals.output:
# What the Fence Knows

The stone fence has forgotten
whose hands laid it, one gray stone
settling into another, moss
doing the slow work of forgetting
softly, so nothing minds.

Down the slope, the barn leans
into its own undoing—
rusty straps let go of beams
the way a hand, in sleep,
releases what it held all day.

I have come to stand here
among the old orchard's crooked elders,
their apples small and bitter now,
dropping unasked into the grass,
feeding what will feed the deer.

The red osier burns its quiet fire
along the ditch, the one bright thing,
insisting on itself in the cold—
not defiance, only this:
the willingness to be red

for as long as red is given.
Nothing here is grieving.
The barn will fall. The fence will spread
its stones like a slow sentence
laid down across the field,

and I will go the way of straps and beams,
the way of fruit that no one gathers.
Let it come. I have seen
how the moss keeps nothing
and is not the poorer for it,

how the osier asks no promise
of another spring,
but stands in the failing light
and holds its color up
against the dark, and is enough.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
